chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## What the company is

Sivers Semiconductors AB (ticker: SIVE.ST; OTC US: SIVEF) is a Swedish holding company with two operating subsidiaries that share almost nothing except a parent. **Sivers Wireless AB** makes millimeter-wave beamformers and antenna modules for SATCOM, 5G/6G, and defense applications, claiming to be the only EU-based commercial provider in several beamformer categories; named customers include the European Space Agency and Intelsat. **Sivers Photonics Ltd.** — the UK subsidiary acquired in 2017 as CST Global — designs custom high-power indium-phosphide distributed-feedback lasers and laser arrays, and it is increasingly positioned as the upstream chokepoint for the External Light Source modules that enable co-packaged optics in next-generation AI data-center GPUs. The two businesses share a balance sheet, a Nasdaq Stockholm listing, and an ambition to dual-list in New York. Everything else — technology, geography, customer base — diverges.

At SEK 72.90 × 311.33 million shares outstanding, the market capitalisation sits at approximately SEK 22.7 billion, or roughly $2.2 billion at current exchange rates. That figure warrants an immediate caveat: analyst writeups circulating in early 2025 cited a market cap of around SEK 3.4 billion — a number that, at the time, may have been accurate but has since been rendered obsolete by a rally that accelerated through the CPO narrative. Readers relying on older secondary sources should reset their mental model accordingly.

## Seventy-five years, three acts

The company was founded in 1951 by engineer Carl von Sivers as Sivers Lab AB, manufacturing passive microwave products and slotted-line VSWR detectors for professional and educational markets. Philips Sweden acquired it in 1960. The entity eventually re-emerged as an independent Stockholm-listed company — Sivers IMA Holding AB — before the two acquisitions that created the modern entity: CST Global in 2017 (the Scottish III-V photonics specialist that became Sivers Photonics) and MixComm in 2022 (a US-based millimeter-wave startup that reinforced the wireless segment). The group rebranded as Sivers Semiconductors AB around the same period. What began as a passive-microwave shop for university labs is now marketing itself to the hyperscalers building out AI compute fabric.

## The management team that matters for the US listing

The 2024 CEO transition is the most readable signal of strategic intent. Vickram Vathulya — PhD from Lehigh, MBA from Berkeley Haas, 25 years across NXP, Maxim, and Nuvotronics — was appointed President and CEO on August 19, 2024, with a personal commitment to purchase up to two million shares at a cost of up to $1 million. The commitment is notable for a company at this stage: public skin in the game by an executive whose remit is explicitly to ready Sivers for a US dual listing. Flanking him is Executive Chairman Bami Bastani, a 42-year semiconductor veteran who has run three public-company turnarounds as CEO and served as an SVP at GlobalFoundries. Bastani joined as Strategic Advisor in August 2023 and moved to Executive Chairman in February 2024. The US-listing architecture is the throughline connecting both appointments.

## FY2025: growth, but deeper losses after accounting restatement

The full-year 2025 results, published in the Annual Report on May 13, 2026, carried an unusual asterisk: they had been restated under PCAOB-aligned standards as preparation for the potential US dual listing.

| Metric | Swedish K3 (original) | PCAOB-restated |
|---|---|---|
| Net sales (SEK M) | 304.1 | 306.6 |
| EBIT (SEK M) | −141.3 | −177.8 |
| Net loss (SEK M) | −186.5 | −222.6 |
| EPS (SEK) | −0.69 | −0.81 |
| Equity per share (SEK) | 3.46 | 3.05 |

Revenue grew 25% year-on-year — 33% at constant currency — to SEK 306.6 million. The sales pipeline expanded 64% to $453 million. Free cash outflow narrowed to SEK 66 million from SEK 151 million in 2022, the improvement that the bull case points to as evidence of operating leverage arriving. Cash at year-end was SEK 43.5 million — thin — topped up by a $17 million term loan and convertible debt in February 2026, and then by a non-dilutive $6.6 million Microelectronics Commons Year 2 grant announced on May 19 for US defense infrastructure work. The restatement widened the operating loss by SEK 36 million through revenue reallocations between periods, inventory revaluations, updated share-based compensation assumptions, and impairment of previously capitalised development expenditure. The accounting revision is operationally neutral, but it reveals that prior-period results were reported under standards more forgiving than what a US listing demands. One Substack analyst who had modeled a bull-case fair value of SEK 14.52 per share — implying the current SEK 72.90 is already more than five times their top scenario — noted at the time that the equity story required a very precise sequencing of customer ramps and margin expansion to justify even that figure.

## The question the rest of this report answers

Is Sivers the next LITE — the chokepoint pattern repeating, where a small western laser maker becomes structurally indispensable as hyperscalers standardize on co-packaged optics — or is the at-the-peak valuation pricing a CPO volume ramp that has not yet shipped a single production module? The June 15, 2026 AGM, where shareholders vote on a 15% dilution authority and a board reshuffle that clears out co-founder Fällström, is the first concrete test of whether management can deliver on the architecture they have been promising since 2024.

chapters.title: From Sivers Lab to Sivers Photonics — 75 years
chapters.body:
## A Passive-Microwave Shop in Stockholm, 1951

Carl von Sivers founded Sivers Lab AB in Sweden in 1951 to make passive microwave components — slotted-line VSWR detectors and the instrumentation that surrounds them. It was artisanal, specialized work, serving defence laboratories and university physics departments across Scandinavia. Nine years later, in 1960, Philips Sweden absorbed the company into its technology portfolio, and Sivers Lab effectively disappeared into a multinational for what would prove to be a long, under-documented interval.

*The precise timeline of the company's re-emergence as an independent entity — the separation from Philips, the eventual listing on Nasdaq Stockholm as Sivers IMA Holding AB — remains a gap in the public record that this chapter flags for further research.* What is clear is that, by the early 2010s, Sivers IMA Holding was a listed Swedish microwave-components house with a heritage brand and a limited growth runway.

## The Foundational Move: CST Global, 2017

Everything that makes Sivers interesting to investors today traces back to a single acquisition. In 2017, Sivers IMA Holding bought [CST Global](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/), a Scottish manufacturer of III-V photonic devices with its own R&D facility and clean-room fabrication capacity outside Glasgow. CST Global supplied photonic components in wafer, coated bar, chip device, and die-on-tape formats — bespoke, low-volume, high-specification work for customers who could not or would not go to the large Asian foundries.

The renamed subsidiary, Sivers Photonics Ltd., gave the group something no amount of microwave-component iteration could have produced: a captive, western-domiciled source of indium phosphide distributed-feedback (InP DFB) lasers. DFB lasers at specific C-band wavelengths (1530–1565 nm) are the light engines inside the transceiver modules that carry data through fibre. In 2017, that was a niche. By 2025 it was a chokepoint.

Two years after the CST deal closed, Sivers Photonics and imec announced a collaboration to integrate C-band InP DFB laser arrays directly onto imec's silicon photonics platform. The work pointed squarely toward the co-packaged optics architecture that hyperscalers would not start seriously deploying for another five years.

## Wireless Expansion and the Rebrand

In 2022, the group acquired MixComm, a US-based millimetre-wave startup, bolting it into the Sivers Wireless AB subsidiary alongside the legacy beamformer and phased-array business. MixComm brought additional customers in 5G fixed wireless, SATCOM, and defence. The group simultaneously began consolidating its identity under a new name: Sivers Semiconductors AB, with two distinct subsidiaries — Sivers Wireless AB (mmWave RF) and Sivers Photonics Ltd. (DFB lasers). The rebrand signalled intent: this was no longer a microwave-instrumentation house but a compound-semiconductor group with a dual-segment story.

## The American Turn

The signals pointing toward a US capital-markets strategy began appearing in mid-2023. In August of that year, Bami Bastani joined the board as a Strategic Advisor — a role notable less for its formal authority than for what it telegraphed. Bastani, a veteran of US semiconductor listings and investor-relations exercises, was elevated to Executive Chairman of Sivers Inc. and Chairman of Sivers AB by February 2024.

Six months later, in August 2024, the group replaced its long-serving CEO. Anders Storm, who had stewarded the company through the CST Global acquisition and the photonics buildout, departed. His successor, Vickram Vathulya — a PhD from Lehigh, an MBA from Berkeley Haas, and an executive with prior roles at Nuvotronics, Maxim, and NXP — brought the profile of a leader hired to speak fluent Wall Street, not just Stureplan.

## 2025–26: The Accounting Signal

Sivers Photonics' FY2025 revenues grew 25% year-on-year to SEK 306.6 million (33% in constant currency). The sales pipeline reached $453 million, up 64%. Those numbers, however, came attached to a caveat: on 13 May 2026, the group published its [2025 Annual Report with PCAOB-restated financials](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/press/sivers-semiconductors-publishes-the-2025-annual-report-adjusting-prior-reported-financials-as-preparation-for-a-potential-dual-listing-in-the-united-states/), explicitly framed as preparation for a potential Nasdaq New York dual listing. The restatement widened the EBIT loss from -SEK 141 million (Swedish K3 standard) to -SEK 178 million — a 26% gap — driven by revenue reallocation, inventory revaluation, share-based compensation fair-value adjustments, and the impairment of capitalised development expenditures. PCAOB adoption is non-trivial overhead for a SEK 22-billion-market-cap growth company; the fact that management chose to absorb it is the clearest commitment signal available.

A $6.6 million NEMC Year 2 grant from the US Department of Defense, announced on 19 May 2026, reinforced the American vector. An AGM scheduled for June 2026 carries a 15% dilution authority vote and a board reshuffle — Joakim Nideborn and Helena Svancar nominated on 20 May — suggesting the capital structure is still being shaped for whatever the dual-listing roadshow requires.

---

Sivers spent roughly 65 years as a passive-microwave shop — first independent, then absorbed into Philips, then independent again — before two acquisitions in five years turned it into what its current management is betting will prove to be a laser chokepoint in the AI optical-interconnect supply chain. The pace of transformation is the story. Whether the underlying technology can execute against a $453 million pipeline while operating losses run at -SEK 178 million annually is the question the rest of this dossier addresses.

chapters.title: Two subsidiaries, two supply chains
chapters.body:
## One competency, two markets

Sivers Semiconductors AB operates through two wholly-owned subsidiaries — Sivers Wireless AB in Stockholm and Sivers Photonics Ltd. in Glasgow — that serve structurally different end-markets yet share a single underlying materials competency: the fabrication of compound III-V semiconductors, primarily indium phosphide (InP) and gallium arsenide (GaAs), into precision radio-frequency and photonic components. That shared substrate is not an accident of corporate history. It is the reason the company exists as a unified entity rather than two separate listings, and it is the foundation on which management's dual-listing thesis rests.

The two segments look almost nothing alike commercially. Wireless sells into long-cycle institutional procurement — space agencies, satellite operators, defense primes — where design wins are slow and revenue is lumpy but durable. Photonics sells into a hypergrowth AI-infrastructure cycle where the purchase decision moves at datacenter speed and the volumes, if they materialise, dwarf anything the wireless book has ever seen. Understanding Sivers requires holding both realities at once.

## Sivers Wireless AB: the institutional floor

The wireless subsidiary is the elder of the two, traceable to the company's 1951 founding as Sivers Lab AB by Carl von Sivers. Today it produces millimetre-wave (mmWave) beamformers, phased-array integrated circuits, and antenna modules for four principal applications: satellite communications (SATCOM), fixed wireless access (FWA), 5G/6G base station infrastructure, and defence and aerospace.

The strongest claim management makes about this segment is that Sivers Wireless is the only EU-based commercial provider of certain beamformer types — specifically those meeting the performance and supply-chain sovereignty requirements of European institutional SATCOM buyers. That claim is difficult to verify independently but is consistent with the named customer roster: the [European Space Agency](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/) and Intelsat. Both represent buyers for whom a European-domiciled supplier with traceable fabrication is not a marketing preference but a procurement requirement. The US equivalent of this logic is now arriving via the Pentagon: a $6.6 million Year 2 grant from the Microelectronics Commons (NEMC) programme, [announced May 19 2026](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/press/sivers-semiconductors-publishes-the-2025-annual-report-adjusting-prior-reported-financials-as-preparation-for-a-potential-dual-listing-in-the-united-states/), specifically for US defence infrastructure modernisation. The NEMC relationship does not yet translate into production revenue, but it establishes Sivers Wireless inside the US Department of Defense supplier ecosystem — a prerequisite for any future prime-contractor relationship.

The wireless segment is not, on its own, a growth story. Its value to the consolidated entity is stability and credibility: recurring institutional customers, a defensible geographic chokepoint in European SATCOM procurement, and now a foothold in US defence that provides non-dilutive grant revenue ($6.6M) while the photonics business scales. Think of it as the cash-burn buffer and strategic legitimacy provider for a business whose real growth vector sits 500 miles northwest, on the outskirts of Glasgow.

## Sivers Photonics Ltd.: the CPO thesis

Sivers Photonics was acquired in 2017 under its previous name, CST Global, and relocated its analytical centre of gravity to the company's equity story sometime around 2022 when co-packaged optics moved from research programme to hyperscaler procurement priority. The subsidiary makes high-power indium phosphide DFB (distributed feedback) lasers, laser arrays, optical amplifiers, and increasingly the External Light Source (ELS) modules that bundle those lasers into a form factor that can be integrated directly into an optical interposer or co-packaged optics assembly.

To understand why this matters, it helps to start at the front of the optical link. At the input of any high-speed optical transceiver — and certainly at the input of a co-packaged optics (CPO) module intended for an AI accelerator package — is a laser. For CPO applications, that laser must satisfy three simultaneous constraints: it must be continuous-wave (CW) rather than pulsed; it must be monochromatic and wavelength-stable (DFB gratings etch a frequency-selective feedback structure into the laser cavity, which locks the emission wavelength to within a fraction of a nanometre); and it must be high-power, because the optical signal will be split across multiple channels, modulated, and transmitted before it reaches its destination. Insufficient power at the source means insufficient signal-to-noise ratio at the detector.

The substrate of choice for these lasers at telecom-band wavelengths — 1.31 microns and 1.55 microns — is indium phosphide. Silicon photonics, which hyperscalers including Intel and Cisco have invested heavily in for integration density, cannot efficiently emit light at these wavelengths. Every silicon photonic chip still needs an external InP laser. Sivers Photonics is one of a small number of independent western foundries capable of custom-designing and small-batch manufacturing these components, which is what positions it as a chokepoint supplier rather than a commodity one.

## Customer architecture in photonics

The photonics customer map reads as an annotated tour of the CPO supply chain. [POET Technologies](https://www.poet-technologies.com/news/poet-technologies-and-sivers-semiconductors-collaborate-on-external-light-sources-for-co-packaged-optics-and-next-generation-ai-market) (NASDAQ/TSX: POET) formalised a strategic collaboration in September 2025, combining Sivers' high-power DFB lasers with POET's optical interposer platform to build ELS modules for CPO and next-generation AI infrastructure. Analyst Tim Savageaux has estimated the annual ELS market at over $1 billion; the broader AI optical connectivity opportunity is typically cited at north of $50 billion. Early POET-Sivers prototypes were targeted for H1 2026; production readiness end-2026.

Ayar Labs, one of the leading silicon-photonic interconnect IP companies for AI hyperscale, uses Sivers DFB laser arrays in its SuperNova multi-wavelength light source — demonstrated publicly together at ECOC 2022. O-Net Communications / Enablence Technologies sources ELS modules with thermal management solutions for CPO. Imec has an ongoing collaboration, begun in 2019, integrating Sivers' C-band InP DFB lasers onto its silicon photonics platform.

Indirectly, the ecosystem reaches further. Marvell acquired Celestial AI — an optical interconnect specialist — in 2025, pulling Sivers-supplied technology into Marvell's AI networking programme. Apple's silicon photonics (SiPH) programme, AMD, Jabil, Lightmatter, and Lightelligence appear in the secondary-source ecosystem map, though none of these represent confirmed direct commercial relationships with Sivers at the frozen snapshot date.

## The LiDAR wildcard

Separate from the CPO thesis, the company has disclosed a strategic automotive FMCW LiDAR customer that is incorporating Sivers photonics technology "across all their platforms," with a production ramp targeted for Q4 2026. The company has put lifecycle revenue for this single customer at $53–138 million over an 8–10 year engagement. At the midpoint — roughly $95 million — that represents approximately 31 percent of FY2025 revenues annualised. At the upper end, $138 million over eight years implies annual revenue that would approximately double the current product revenue line of SEK 85.7 million.

The customer has not been named publicly, which makes independent verification impossible at this stage. The range itself — $53M to $138M — is unusually wide for a company citing specific platform-level design wins, which suggests either significant uncertainty in volume forecasting or deliberate obfuscation to protect a sensitive commercial relationship. Q4 2026 production is the first concrete checkpoint; if that ramp slips or the customer reduces platform scope, the LiDAR thesis evaporates quickly.

## The financial picture — and its gaps

One analytical frustration is that Sivers does not publish a clean segment revenue split. FY2025 total revenues came in at SEK 306.6 million under PCAOB restatement, up 25 percent reported and 33 percent in constant currency — but product revenue of SEK 85.7 million grew only 13 percent at constant FX. The gap between total revenue growth (33%) and product revenue growth (13%) implies that a significant and growing portion of consolidated revenues derives from service contracts, licensing arrangements, and funded development agreements rather than shipped components. That structure is not inherently problematic — development funding is non-dilutive and often de-risks production transitions — but it makes the segment-level revenue story opaque. Readers drawing conclusions about wireless versus photonics commercial momentum from aggregate numbers should treat those inferences as approximate.

| Metric | FY2024 (PCAOB) | FY2025 (PCAOB) | YoY |
|---|---|---|---|
| Net sales (SEK m) | 219.2 | 306.6 | +40% |
| Product revenue (SEK m) | — | 85.7 | +13% (const. FX) |
| EBIT (SEK m) | — | –177.8 | — |
| Net loss (SEK m) | –183.9 | –222.6 | wider |
| Cash at year-end (SEK m) | 18.0 | 43.5 | — |

Note: FY2024 revenue was restated downward (SEK 243.7M → SEK 219.2M) under PCAOB rules, and FY2024 losses widened. This is consistent with the company's stated restatement driver of reallocating revenues between periods.

## The segment-level verdict

The cleanest summary is structural: Sivers Wireless is the historical floor and the institutional credibility anchor. Its European sovereign-supply position for SATCOM-grade beamformers, a pair of named space-sector customers, and an emerging US defence pipeline via NEMC provide recurring revenue and strategic positioning that would be hard to replicate quickly — but the ceiling is limited by the pace of European space procurement and 5G infrastructure rollout. Sivers Photonics is the option value: a sub-$2B listed company with direct design-win relationships across the emergent CPO supply chain, an automotive LiDAR wildcard that could independently justify the current valuation if the Q4 2026 production ramp delivers, and a pipeline that grew 64 percent year-on-year to $453 million. The financial result reflects this structure: wireless funds the building; photonics is the reason anyone is in the room.

chapters.title: Two sets of books — and what the restatement actually means
chapters.body:
## The restatement in plain language

On 13 May 2026, Sivers Semiconductors published its 2025 Annual Report — nearly three months after preliminary results had already circulated. The delay was not accidental. Embedded in the document was a disclosure that should arrest any investor treating the prior numbers as a baseline: a full PCAOB-aligned restatement of both FY2025 and FY2024, prepared as groundwork for a potential US dual listing. The effect was material. The EBIT loss for FY2025 widened by SEK 36.5 million. The net loss deepened by SEK 36.1 million. Book equity fell by SEK 127 million. And the FY2024 figures — already unattractive — were revised to look considerably worse.

Two sets of books now exist. Neither is wrong in a legal sense: Swedish K3 accounting, which Sivers has always reported under, permits practices that PCAOB does not. But for investors evaluating the company on a pre-listing basis, the PCAOB-restated figures are the ones that matter for comparability with US-listed peers. They are also the more conservative set.

| Metric | As Reported (K3) | PCAOB-Restated | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Net Sales (SEK M) | 304.1 | 306.6 | +2.5 |
| EBIT (SEK M) | −141.3 | −177.8 | −36.5 |
| Net Result (SEK M) | −186.5 | −222.6 | −36.1 |
| EPS (SEK) | −0.69 | −0.81 | −0.12 |
| Equity (SEK M) | 1,076.8 | 949.8 | −127.0 |
| Equity/Share (SEK) | 3.46 | 3.05 | −0.41 |

*FY2025 — [Sivers 2025 Annual Report](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/press/sivers-semiconductors-publishes-the-2025-annual-report-adjusting-prior-reported-financials-as-preparation-for-a-potential-dual-listing-in-the-united-states/)*

Revenue, curiously, moved slightly upward under PCAOB (SEK 304.1M → SEK 306.6M). That is not a comfort. It reflects the timing mechanics of the restatement: revenue was reallocated *out of* 2024 and *into* 2025, with some portion pushed further out to 2026 and beyond. Sivers' historical top line was worse than it appeared; its current period looks marginally better partly as an artifact of that reallocation.

## The five levers — and which one cuts deepest

The company disclosed five specific restatement drivers. Taken in order of analytical importance:

**Development capitalization impairment** is the most consequential. Swedish K3 accounting allows companies to capitalise R&D spending as a balance-sheet asset when commercial viability is assessed as probable. PCAOB applies a stricter standard: the threshold for recognising such capitalised costs is higher, and absent sufficient commercial evidence — signed volume commitments, for instance, rather than letters of intent — the asset must be expensed. Sivers had capitalised meaningful development expenditures under K3. The PCAOB restatement effectively says: not yet. The SEK 127-million reduction in book equity is the cumulative balance-sheet footprint of this reclassification. For a company whose equity coverage story depends heavily on the asset base supporting its laser platform, the haircut is not trivial.

**Revenue reallocation between periods** is conceptually simpler but historically damaging. Under PCAOB revenue recognition standards, certain contracts or milestone payments that K3 had recognised in FY2024 did not yet meet the criteria for recognition. The result is a FY2024 revenue revision from SEK 243.7M down to SEK 219.2M — a reduction of SEK 24.5 million, or roughly 10% of what was reported. More strikingly, the FY2024 net loss was revised from SEK 116.3M to SEK 183.9M — a SEK 67.6 million widening. Investors who benchmarked Sivers' loss trajectory against the K3 numbers have been working from a flattering baseline. The underlying deterioration in FY2024 was substantially larger than reported.

**Inventory revaluation** and **share-based compensation fair value updates** are more mechanical in nature. Inventory write-downs under PCAOB's lower-of-cost-or-net-realisable-value tests tend to be applied more conservatively than under K3; the fair value methodology for equity-settled awards follows US GAAP conventions that can produce different expense recognition patterns. Neither driver is unusual in a dual-listing restatement context. Both add to the cumulative EBIT drag.

**Income statement reclassification from by-nature to by-function** reshapes presentation rather than outcomes — R&D, COGS, and G&A are recut so US-style investors can read gross margin and operating leverage directly. This does not change the total loss, but it changes how analysts model it.

## What five years of growth actually looks like

Strip away the accounting complexity and the underlying trajectory is, at minimum, real. Revenue has grown at a 36.7% CAGR from 2016 to 2025, a roughly 16x expansion over the decade, per analyst estimates at [Global Equity Briefing](https://www.globalequitybriefing.com/p/sivers-semiconductors-hype-or-asymmetric). Free cash outflow has narrowed from SEK 151 million in FY2022 to SEK 66 million in FY2025. Operating margin improved from -83% (FY2022) to -39% (FY2025). The direction of travel is correct. The absolute level remains heavily negative.

Q4 FY2025 adds granularity. Standalone revenue of SEK 80.7M was up 5% year-on-year at reported rates, but 17% in constant currency — a meaningful divergence reflecting SEK appreciation. Product revenue of SEK 21.3M grew 13% quarter-on-quarter. Annualised from the Q4 run rate, revenue would be approximately SEK 320M — slightly below what the company's stated pipeline trajectory might suggest, but not inconsistent with a business in active customer qualification rather than high-volume production. The qualification-to-revenue lag in laser supply chains runs six to eighteen months from design-in to purchase order; Q4 product revenue is the seed of what may follow.

## Capital structure: the cost of survival

Sivers has funded its growth primarily through equity issuance. Since 2020, shares outstanding have increased by 101.58% — essentially, the share count doubled. Year-end FY2025 cash stood at SEK 43.5M against annual FCF consumption of SEK 66M: roughly three quarters of runway, give or take, before the next financing event.

The recent financing sequence tells its own story. A SEK 95M rights issue in 2025 diluted existing holders by approximately 8%. In February 2026, the company raised $17M via a term loan and convertible instrument — a structure that carries dilution optionality embedded in the convertible leg. In May 2026, it secured a $6.6M non-dilutive grant under the US Department of Defense's Microelectronics Commons NEMC Year 2 programme, earmarked for defence infrastructure modernisation. The grant is genuinely non-dilutive, but at current burn rates it covers roughly one quarter of FCF.

The June 15 Annual General Meeting will ask shareholders to authorise the issuance of up to 53,844,956 new shares — approximately 15% of current shares outstanding — covering warrants, convertibles, and any future ordinary share issuances. A separate proposal covers a 2% long-term incentive plan (approximately 7 million Class C options). Management has cited four stated uses: organic growth funding, potential M&A, strategic shareholder onboarding, and US listing enablement. A 15% authority does not compel immediate drawdown, but it sets the ceiling on what the board can issue before returning to shareholders. For a company that has doubled its share count in five years, any authorisation of this scope deserves scrutiny.

## The valuation arithmetic

At SEK 72.90 — a five-year high, touched during the research window — Sivers' market capitalisation is approximately SEK 22.7 billion, or roughly $2.2 billion at prevailing exchange rates. Against PCAOB-restated FY2025 revenue of SEK 306.6M, that is a price-to-sales multiple of approximately **74x**.

The substack analyst whose work informed this dossier constructed a bull-case 2030 model: 45% revenue CAGR, 25% operating margin, SEK 2.3 billion revenue, SEK 404 million net income. On those assumptions — which are generous — the analyst's implied fair value is SEK 14.52 per share. The current price is SEK 72.90: roughly five times that bull-case estimate.

The gap is not necessarily irrational in a market pricing optionality on co-packaged optics adoption. But it does mean the market is either assuming a considerably more aggressive ramp than the analyst's model, a higher terminal margin, or a non-trivial probability of acquisition at a strategic premium. It is not pricing a business at its operational fundamentals as they currently exist.

## The frame for what follows

The PCAOB restatement resolves one question and opens another. The resolved question is which set of numbers an investor should use: the restated figures are the right baseline, and they show a company that lost SEK 222.6M on SEK 306.6M of revenue in FY2025. The open question is whether the narrative that justifies SEK 22.7B in market capitalisation — CPO production beginning end-2026, a $453M pipeline growing 64% year-on-year, a US listing that re-rates the stock against American comparables — will be validated by shipped product and cash-generating customer ramps, or whether it will dissolve under the weight of further dilution, delayed qualification timelines, and a laser market that is less concentrated than the bull case assumes.

The financials show a company that is **real** — the growth is there, the margin improvement is there, the pipeline has names attached to it. They also show a company that is **under-funded** for the ambition it is selling — three quarters of cash, a 15% dilution proposal, and a convertible overhang. And they show a company valued for a scenario that has **not yet shipped**. The chapters that follow examine the technology, the customer ramps, and the competitive position to assess whether that gap closes — or widens.

chapters.title: The five quarters that built the rally
chapters.body:
The stock spent most of 2023 and 2024 trading below SEK 5. Then, in the eighteen months that followed the arrival of a new chief executive, it ran to SEK 72.90 — a 40-fold move from its five-year floor of SEK 1.80, placing a market capitalisation of roughly SEK 22.7 billion (approximately $2.2 billion) on a company that lost SEK 178 million on SEK 307 million of revenue in its most recent fiscal year. The move demands explanation. Five quarters supply most of it.

## August 2024: The handover

The starting gun was quiet. On 19 August 2024, Sivers announced that Anders Storm was stepping down and that Vickram Vathulya — with a background in optical networking and photonics commercialisation — would take the helm. Vathulya did not immediately change the financial trajectory. FY2024 results, as originally reported under Swedish K3 accounting standards, showed net sales of SEK 243.7 million and a net loss of SEK 116.3 million. But he signalled a sharper commercial focus on co-packaged optics, repositioning the photonics narrative away from generic "laser supplier" framing and toward a specific upstream slot in the AI datacenter supply chain. The language in investor materials shifted; so did the pipeline composition.

## H1 2025: Rights issue and the quiet build

The first half of 2025 brought necessary but dilutive housekeeping. A SEK 95 million rights issue — roughly 8% dilution — kept the balance sheet viable while Vathulya reshaped the commercial book. The broader capital context was sobering: shares outstanding have more than doubled since 2020, a 101% dilution that reflects the cost of surviving a decade-long pre-profitability growth phase. Free cash outflow, which had reached SEK 151 million as recently as 2022, compressed to SEK 66 million by year-end 2025 — real improvement, though the company ended the year with only SEK 43.5 million of cash on hand.

The wireless segment — mmWave beamformers for satellite communications customers including the European Space Agency and Intelsat — continued to carry product revenue. But investor attention was migrating toward photonics, and toward what Sivers could mean for co-packaged optics specifically.

## September 29, 2025: The POET anchor

The inflection moment arrived at the end of the third quarter. On 29 September 2025, Sivers and [POET Technologies](https://www.poet-technologies.com/news/poet-technologies-and-sivers-semiconductors-collaborate-on-external-light-sources-for-co-packaged-optics-and-next-generation-ai-market) announced a strategic collaboration to build External Light Source modules combining Sivers' high-power InP DFB lasers with POET's Optical Interposer platform. The deal was more than a supplier agreement: it contractually anchored Sivers' position in a specific CPO architecture at the moment CPO was becoming a central topic in AI infrastructure planning.

Vathulya framed the rationale directly:

> "We see a highly complementary fit between our high-performance DFB lasers and POET's innovative optical interposer platform."

Analyst Tim Savageaux had placed the ELS market opportunity at over $1 billion annually. The POET deal made Sivers the referenced laser supplier for one of the higher-profile bets in that space. When Ayar Labs' SuperNova — a multi-wavelength light source that uses Sivers laser arrays, jointly demonstrated at ECOC 2022 — gained traction in specialist AI infrastructure publications, the Sivers name travelled with it. The stock accelerated through Q4 2025 and into the new year. The pipeline closed the year at $453 million, up 64% year-on-year.

## February 26, 2026: The preliminary read

The Q4 2025 preliminary results, published 26 February, offered incremental validation without a headline breakout. Fourth-quarter net sales reached SEK 80.7 million, up just 5% year-on-year on a reported basis — but up 17% at constant currency, a gap that reflects SEK appreciation rather than operational weakness. Product revenue grew 13% quarter-on-quarter to SEK 21.3 million. Full-year 2025 net sales under K3 came to SEK 304.1 million; the operating loss was SEK 141.3 million.

Two weeks later, the company disclosed a $17 million financing package combining a term loan and convertible debt — a reminder that at SEK 43.5 million of year-end cash, the runway was measured in months, not years.

## May 13, 2026: The restatement that didn't crater anything

The annual report, published 13 May 2026, was the most consequential document in the sequence. It carried PCAOB-aligned restated financials — a prerequisite for a planned US dual listing — and the revisions were not cosmetic. The FY2025 EBIT loss widened by SEK 36 million, from SEK 141.3 million to SEK 177.8 million. Net loss moved from SEK 186.5 million to SEK 222.6 million; EPS fell from SEK -0.69 to SEK -0.81. Restatement drivers included revenue reallocation between periods, revised inventory valuations, updated share-based compensation fair values, and impairment of previously capitalised development expenditure.

| Period | Revenue (SEK M) | EBIT (SEK M) | Net loss (SEK M) |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2024 (K3 as reported) | 243.7 | n/d | -116.3 |
| FY2024 (PCAOB restated) | 219.2 | n/d | -183.9 |
| FY2025 (K3 as reported) | 304.1 | -141.3 | -186.5 |
| FY2025 (PCAOB restated) | 306.6 | -177.8 | -222.6 |

The stock barely moved. That non-reaction is itself a data point about who now holds the shares. Institutional readers with experience of PCAOB-conversion exercises interpreted the restatement as accounting plumbing ahead of an SEC process — not operational deterioration. The restatement simultaneously reduced FY2024 revenue by SEK 24.5 million and widened the 2024 net loss by SEK 67.6 million, erasing what had looked like a more modest prior-year result. Revenue growth from 2024 to 2025 looks better under the restated figures: SEK 219.2 million to SEK 306.6 million, a 40% increase.

Six days later, a $6.6 million Year 2 grant arrived from the US Department of Defense's Microelectronics Commons program — non-dilutive capital that doubles as a sovereignty-of-supply endorsement timed precisely as the company readied its US listing case.

## The MSCI trigger and the test ahead

Sivers joins the MSCI Sweden Small Cap Index effective 29 May 2026 — the same date Q1 2026 results are scheduled (delayed from an earlier target). Passive funds tracking the index must buy shares regardless of what those results contain. The simultaneity is either fortuitous or a reminder that corporate calendars are never entirely accidental.

The rally has been built on genuine operational improvement — FCF cut from -SEK 151 million to -SEK 66 million over three years, revenue compounding at 36.7% annually since 2016, a pipeline that has grown 16-fold over a decade. But what is not yet real, in any material shipped-and-invoiced sense, is co-packaged optics revenue. The POET ELS modules remain in early prototype phase, with production readiness targeted for end-2026. The unnamed automotive LiDAR customer, whose eight-to-ten year lifecycle value is estimated at $53–138 million, has a production ramp planned for Q4 2026 — still ahead. At SEK 72.90, one detailed bull-case model implies a 2030 fair value closer to SEK 14.52, suggesting the market is pricing a substantially more aggressive ramp and higher terminal margins than even optimistic projections support. The next two to three quarters need to convert that $453 million pipeline into production-stage revenue — not further partnership announcements. The thesis is coherent. The factory has not yet been asked to prove it.

chapters.title: The team that is going to ring the Nasdaq bell
chapters.body:
## The Architect and His Timeline

The appointments did not arrive by coincidence. In August 2023, Bami Bastani joined Sivers Semiconductors as a Strategic Advisor — a title that, in semiconductor circles, rarely means what it says. By February 2024 he was Executive Chairman of the US subsidiary and Chairman of the Swedish parent. Six months later, a new CEO arrived. Eighteen months after that, the company filed PCAOB-aligned restated financials — the accounting standard required for a US public listing — and simultaneously nominated two new directors whose CVs read like a cross-border transaction checklist. The sequence is not coincidental. It is a programme.

Bastani is the architect. Forty-two years in the semiconductor industry have taken him from component roles at Intel and National Semiconductor through systems-on-chip at Fujitsu Micro to three separate tenures as a turnaround CEO at public companies: ANADIGICS, a III-V compound semiconductor maker that Wall Street had given up on; Trident Microsystems, a digital media chipmaker navigating a brutal cost cycle; and Meru Networks, an enterprise WiFi platform. Each was a listed company. Each required restructuring under quarterly earnings scrutiny. His final corporate role before arriving at Sivers was Senior Vice President at GlobalFoundries, the world's third-largest foundry, where he also served on the board of the Global Semiconductor Alliance. He is, in short, not a board ornament. He is the most experienced operating executive in the room, placed at the chairman seat specifically to translate a Swedish mid-cap photonics company into something a Nasdaq investor relations roadshow can sell.

## The CEO Who Invested in His Own Bet

Vickram Vathulya was appointed President and CEO on 19 August 2024, replacing Anders Storm. His credentials are unusual for a Stockholm-listed company: a PhD in Electrical Engineering from Lehigh University in Pennsylvania, an MBA from Berkeley Haas, and twenty-five years in semiconductors spanning geographies that track the industry's centre of gravity rather than Stockholm's. At NXP Semiconductors he ran RF and wireless business lines; at Maxim Integrated he grew the RF and wireless portfolio; at Maxim Semiconductors he revitalised what the company described as its "largest and most profitable" standard products division. His most recent pre-Sivers role was President of Nuvotronics, a compound-semiconductor and advanced-interconnect company, where he led what the company called a strategic, operational and cultural transformation.

> "We see a highly complementary fit between our high-performance DFB lasers and POET's innovative optical interposer platform," [Vathulya told the market](https://www.poet-technologies.com/news/poet-technologies-and-sivers-semiconductors-collaborate-on-external-light-sources-for-co-packaged-optics-and-next-generation-ai-market) at the announcement of the POET Technologies partnership in September 2025.

What distinguishes the appointment beyond the CV is the share commitment. At the time of his appointment, Vathulya agreed to subscribe to up to two million Sivers shares, subject to shareholder approval — a personal commitment valued at up to $1 million at prevailing prices. For a CEO inheriting an operating loss of SEK 177.8 million against revenue of SEK 306.6 million in fiscal 2025, that is not a symbolic gesture. A Lehigh PhD and Berkeley MBA running a Swedish-listed compound semiconductor company is not, as one analyst framing puts it, staffed for European institutional comfort. It is staffed for a Nasdaq investor day.

## The Door Was Already Open

The board member whose significance is most easily underweighted is Todd Thomson — and that would be a mistake. Thomson joined the Sivers board in 2021, three years before Bastani arrived and four years before the PCAOB restatement that crystallised the US-listing trajectory. That sequence matters: Thomson did not follow Bastani onto the board. If anything, he preceded him.

His CV is the most concentrated source of US capital-markets credibility on the board. He holds an MBA from Wharton and a BA in Economics from Davidson College. At Citigroup he served as CFO for five years, then as CEO of Citigroup Global Wealth Management — a $10 billion division — for two and a half years, and subsequently as CEO of Citigroup Alternative Investments. He chaired the Citi Pension Investment Committee. Before Citi, his career ran through Bain & Company, Booz Allen Hamilton, Barents Group and GE Capital, with advisory work at GlobalFoundries providing the semiconductor-specific thread. He currently serves as COO and CFO of Kairos Ventures, a US venture capital firm, and sits on the board of Actuate Therapeutics, as well as investment committees at Davidson College, the World Resources Institute and Dynasty.

A former Citi CFO who has served on investment committees at three institutions and currently runs the finances of a US VC firm does not join the board of a Stockholm small-cap to provide passive oversight. The Bastani-Vathulya-Thomson combination is unusually heavy on US public-company experience for a company at this market capitalisation — approximately SEK 22.7 billion, or roughly $2.2 billion at current exchange rates — and the concentration is deliberate. Thomson, in all probability, was the figure who opened the door.

## The Technical Floor

Karin Raj is not a finance professional, which is precisely the point. As CTO Europe at Nokia — an organisation that has navigated every major inflection point in wireless infrastructure from 2G through 5G — she carries direct operational authority in the exact intersection of domains Sivers sells into: telecommunications, satellite communications, semiconductors, photonics, sensors and nanotechnology. Her career has taken her through Ericsson and across geographies including the United States, China, India, France, Turkey and the Nordic countries. She led technical functions through multiple wireless-generation transitions and has domain exposure in AI, IoT and high-precision micro-mechanics.

At Sivers she chairs the Investment Committee — the board subcommittee with authority over capital expenditure decisions. That is the structural CTO function of the board: independent technical review of whether the product roadmap and capex allocation are coherent with what the market will actually require. For a company whose central thesis rests on the claim that InP DFB lasers are the irreplaceable upstream component in the co-packaged optics supply chain, having a sitting Nokia CTO Europe making the capex calls is not decoration. It is the credibility mechanism that keeps the roadmap honest.

## The Departures Are Not Symmetrical

Fällström leaves the board alongside two other directors: Tomas Duffy and Keith Halsey. But the three departures are not equivalent, and treating them as a bloc obscures what each represents.

Tomas Duffy is the institutional memory. He joined the Sivers board in 2016, became Chairman in 2018, and was present at every major structural decision in the company's modern history: the 2017 acquisition of CST Global (which became Sivers Photonics, the UK-based laser operation); the 2022 acquisition of MixComm; and the rebranding from Sivers IMA to Sivers Semiconductors. His pre-Sivers career at EKN Exportkreditnämnden — the Swedish state export credit agency, where he served as Director of Large Corporates and Head of Telecom from December 2010 to April 2017 — anchored the company's European institutional credibility through the growth-stage years when Swedish government-adjacent credibility mattered for access to capital and contracts. He holds a BSc from KTH, the Royal Institute of Technology, and retains concurrent board seats at CST Global Ltd., Stella Tech AB and Stella Tech Distribution AB. His departure is not a finding of fault. The transition to a US-listing-architect chairman made him surplus to the next phase rather than wrong for the previous one.

Erik Fällström's departure is different in character. He is a co-founder, currently CEO of DDM Debt, and controls approximately 11.8 per cent of Sivers' voting rights through DDM and the Fällström Family Office — a stake he retains after leaving the board. DDM has publicly stated that it wishes to drive Sivers "toward a broader investment company," a strategic vision in direct tension with the focused-operating-company narrative that a Nasdaq listing requires. Activist holding-company framing and a Nasdaq IPO pitch are incompatible. His departure from the board clears the room for a story Sivers can actually tell on a US roadshow; his continuing economic stake means the strategic tension does not disappear, it relocates to the shareholder register.

Keith Halsey was elected to the board at the 15 May 2024 AGM and is departing approximately thirteen months later. Public biographical detail on Halsey remains thin in the sources reviewed at the snapshot date — this is a genuine sourcing gap, not a basis for inference. The short tenure is consistent with a transitional appointment bridging the pre-Bastani board configuration and the US-listing-prep composition, but the AGM materials do not offer an explanation for his rotation, and speculation would outrun the available evidence.

## The Incoming Slate

Joakim Nideborn, nominated as Vice Chairman, is not a "broad CFO background" abstraction — he is the sitting CFO and Deputy CEO of HMS Networks AB, a Nasdaq Stockholm-listed industrial communications company where he has served since December 2017, with promotion to Deputy CEO in December 2021. His prior career ran through Axiell Group, Ixyz Consulting and Beijer Electronics. His stated focus at Sivers is primary oversight of the board for Nordic-region customers, employees and investors — the governance counterpart to Bastani's US-capital-markets orientation.

Helena Svancar is the most cross-border M&A-pedigreed director on the incoming board. She spent ten years at Deutsche Bank, rising to Managing Director and Head of Corporate Finance Nordics, then nearly five years as Head of M&A at Ericsson before joining Verdane, the Nordic growth-equity firm, as a Partner in September 2022. She holds a CEMS MSc in Finance and International Management from Stockholm School of Economics and the University of St. Gallen, and currently serves as a non-executive director at Onomondo and at Truecaller, where she chairs the Remuneration Committee. A former Deutsche Bank Head of Corporate Finance Nordics and former Ericsson M&A chief is the addition a board makes when it expects to execute cross-border transactions. Her appointment is signal-dense.

## Overhang

Two concurrent governance concerns shadow the AGM. Sweden's Economic Crime Authority (Ekobrottsmyndigheten) is examining possible market abuse violations connected to the Nasdaq dual-listing announcement, which leaked approximately forty-eight hours early via an anonymous account on X. The investigation is open as of the snapshot date; its outcome could materially affect investor sentiment in the weeks surrounding the listing mechanics. Separately, Sivers joins the MSCI Sweden Small Cap Index on 29 May 2026 — the same date Q1 results land under the new PCAOB reporting regime. Passive fund buying is mechanically forced to coincide with the first earnings release in the new accounting framework. That is an unusual collision of technical and fundamental catalysts, and it is not clear which will dominate.

## The Shape of the Board

Post-AGM, the Sivers board numbers five: Bastani as Executive Chairman, Vathulya running the operation from the CEO seat, Nideborn as Vice Chairman with Nordic-governance oversight, Thomson as the most credentialed US capital-markets figure on the board, and Raj as the technical anchor and Investment Committee chair. Svancar adds the M&A and cross-border transaction capability.

The Swedish founder-investor presence — Fällström's strategic vision for a holding company, Duffy's European institutional credibility function — is being cleared out. The shape that remains says Nasdaq New York. Four of the five directors carry primary professional identities in corporate-finance and transactional execution. For a company at approximately $2.2 billion market capitalisation, that concentration of financial-markets pedigree is not an accident of hiring. The only question the board composition leaves open is timing.

chapters.title: Where Sivers sits in the AI photonics stack
chapters.body:
## The layer that doesn't ship to hyperscalers

Investors in Sivers Semiconductors AB sometimes speak as though the company has a direct line into Microsoft's data-centre procurement. It does not. Understanding where Sivers actually sits in the stack — and what that position is worth commercially — is the single most analytically productive exercise in evaluating the company's $453 million pipeline.

The co-packaged optics supply chain runs in layers. At the top sit the hyperscalers: Microsoft, Meta, Amazon Web Services, Google. Below them are the GPU and accelerator vendors — NVIDIA, AMD, Marvell, Broadcom — whose silicon defines the interconnect specifications. Below that is the critical integration layer that the market has only recently begun to scrutinise: the CPO module integrators — POET Technologies, Ayar Labs, Lightmatter, Lightelligence, Celestial AI — whose job is to assemble optical interposers and External Light Source modules compact and efficient enough to sit inside a next-generation AI accelerator package. It is at this layer that the laser question becomes urgent. And it is here, one rung below, that Sivers operates.

Sivers Photonics — the UK-based subsidiary acquired in 2017 as CST Global — manufactures Indium Phosphide DFB lasers and laser arrays. Those components ship not to Microsoft or NVIDIA but to the design houses at the CPO integration layer. Those design houses are the gatekeepers. Whether Sivers' chokepoint position converts to revenue depends entirely on which of its design-house customers wins which hyperscaler design slot — a decision one step outside Sivers' control.

## POET: the most consequential named partnership

On 29 September 2025, Sivers and POET Technologies issued a joint press release announcing a strategic collaboration to develop External Light Source modules for co-packaged optics and the broader AI infrastructure market. The two companies characterised the arrangement as combining Sivers' high-power DFB lasers with POET's Optical Interposer platform — an architecture that embeds III-V light sources into a planar semiconductor structure, replacing discrete fibre connections at the package level.

The commercial logic is straightforward: POET brings the integration substrate; Sivers brings the laser that illuminates it. The target market, per analyst Tim Savageaux, is a $1 billion-plus annual ELS market, sitting inside a broader AI optical connectivity opportunity that multiple parties estimate above $50 billion.

The timeline is tighter than it sounds. Sivers' CEO Vickram Vathulya stated at announcement:

> "We see a highly complementary fit between our high-performance DFB lasers and POET's innovative optical interposer platform."

POET's Executive Chairman and CEO, Dr Suresh Venkatesan, framed the strategic rationale from the integrator's side:

> "Modules optimized for size, performance and cost — exactly what the CPO and AI markets demand."

Early prototypes are targeted for the first half of 2026; production readiness is projected for end of 2026. Both timelines remain to be confirmed by engineering results. POET is a small-cap stock listed on both NASDAQ and the TSX, with its own execution risk. The partnership is real — the product roadmap is aspirational until hardware ships at yield.

## Ayar Labs: the longer, quieter relationship

The Ayar Labs relationship is structurally different from POET's. It predates the current CPO investment cycle and has been demonstrated in public technical forums. At the European Conference on Optical Communications in 2022, Sivers and Ayar jointly showcased DFB laser arrays integrated into Ayar's SuperNova multi-wavelength light source — the optical engine at the centre of Ayar's hyperscale AI interconnect proposition.

The SuperNova is widely regarded as one of the most technically advanced commercial CPO light-source candidates. Ayar Labs, a private company, has disclosed engagement with several hyperscale customers without naming them publicly. Its silicon photonics platform targets in-package optical I/O for AI accelerators — a use case that requires a stable, high-power, thermally consistent C-band light source at the laser foundry level. That is precisely the capability Sivers offers through its Glasgow foundry.

The Ayar relationship matters for two reasons. First, it is a multi-year demonstrated supplier arrangement, not a press-release bilateral. Second, if Ayar wins a design slot with a major hyperscaler, Sivers laser arrays are plausibly inside that win. That indirect exposure is analytically real — it just cannot be stated as a confirmed customer relationship, because Sivers has not confirmed it.

## O-Net/Enablence and the thermal constraint

The third named design-house customer is O-Net Communications, working through its Enablence Technologies subsidiary on ELS modules with integrated thermal solutions for CPO. Thermal management is not a secondary concern in co-packaged optics: laser performance degrades meaningfully with temperature, and the thermal environment inside a tightly integrated GPU package is severe. Yield loss at thermal qualification is one of the primary reasons CPO module production has not yet scaled to hyperscaler procurement volumes.

The O-Net relationship is lower-profile than POET, and O-Net as a mid-cap Chinese company carries its own geopolitical and commercial risks that any investor building a western-supply-chain thesis around Sivers should weigh explicitly.

## imec: the structural endorsement

Before the CPO narrative took hold, Sivers had already established the more technically significant validation that tends to get underweighted in the current hype cycle: a joint development programme with imec — Belgium's microelectronics research consortium and the European reference centre for silicon photonics — that began in 2019. The collaboration integrates C-band InP DFB lasers (operating across the 1,530 to 1,565 nanometre window) onto imec's silicon photonics platform.

imec does not partner casually. Its silicon photonics programme feeds directly into European and US industrialisation programmes for next-generation photonic integrated circuits. A seven-year integration collaboration with imec is a better proxy for the maturity of Sivers' laser technology than any individual commercial press release.

## The wireless and defence customers: a different revenue profile

The photonics stack dominates the AI narrative, but Sivers' wireless segment — housed in Sivers Wireless AB — holds the company's most concretely disclosed revenue commitments. The European Space Agency and Intelsat are named customers for millimetre-wave beamformer hardware used in satellite communications. In May 2026, the US Department of Defense awarded Sivers $6.6 million in Year 2 funding through the Microelectronics Commons programme, supporting domestic defence electronics infrastructure.

The single largest disclosed revenue potential sits with an unnamed automotive LiDAR customer that has committed to deploying Sivers technology "across all their platforms." Analyst estimates for this relationship put the lifecycle revenue at $53 million to $138 million over an eight-to-ten-year period — equivalent to 16 to 44 per cent of FY2025 total revenue of SEK 306.6 million. Production is projected to begin in Q4 2026. Like the CPO partnerships, this remains a forward commitment until the first units ship and are accepted.

## Concentration risk and the pipeline caveat

The $453 million pipeline Sivers disclosed for FY2025 — a 64 per cent year-on-year increase — is distributed across these named partnerships and undisclosed parties. No single customer has been identified as exceeding 25 per cent of that figure. The diversification, on its face, looks like a positive.

The analytical problem is what lies upstream of Sivers. POET is a small-cap company with its own funding pressures. Ayar Labs is private and pre-revenue at hyperscaler scale. O-Net carries cross-border risk. The entire commercial layer that Sivers supplies is itself in early-stage commercialisation. A pipeline distributed across customers who are not yet at scale is not the same as a pipeline distributed across customers who are shipping at volume.

The implied indirect exposure through these design houses — to Marvell (via its 2025 acquisition of Celestial AI), to AMD, to Lightmatter, to Lightelligence — is analytically interesting but should be treated as structural optionality, not as disclosed revenue exposure. Sivers has not confirmed any of these as direct customer relationships.

## The validation test

There is a clean standard for what would confirm the commercial thesis. If NVIDIA, Microsoft, Meta, or Amazon were to name Sivers — directly or by naming one of its design-house customers in a hyperscale optical-interconnect announcement — the supply-chain position would convert from technically plausible to commercially validated. As of 23 May 2026, none of this has happened.

Sivers' chokepoint is real in a narrow technical sense: there are very few independent western InP DFB laser foundries with the combination of C-band performance, power density, and volume capability that CPO integration demands. The Glasgow facility, inherited from CST Global, occupies a structurally scarce position. But scarcity is a necessary condition for pricing power, not a sufficient one. Whether the chokepoint translates into revenue — and at what margin — depends on decisions being made one layer above Sivers, by companies that are themselves racing to win designs from customers that have not yet committed to CPO at production volumes. The company is the right answer to a question the market is still deciding whether to ask.

chapters.title: Why the comparison is COHR and LITE, but the analog is something smaller
chapters.body:
## The Scale Gap Is Not the Point

The first instinct when a European semiconductor company announces US dual-listing preparations is to benchmark it against the American-listed incumbents in the same vertical. In co-packaged optics, that reflex leads directly to Coherent Corp. (COHR) and Lumentum (LITE) — two companies that in March 2026 received a combined $2 billion in simultaneous strategic investments from NVIDIA, a vote of confidence that rippled through every laser and transceiver stock on both sides of the Atlantic.

The size comparison is arresting. Coherent reported quarterly revenue of approximately $1.81 billion in its most recently disclosed quarter, implying an annualised run-rate above $7 billion. Lumentum's comparable figure was roughly $808 million per quarter, tracking above $3 billion annually. MACOM Technology Solutions — a third US-listed photonics semi that frequently appears in the same analyst notes — generates approximately $700 million annually. Against these: Sivers Semiconductors reported full-year 2025 net sales of SEK 306.6 million, approximately $33 million at prevailing exchange rates. Sivers is roughly 1% of Lumentum's revenue base and less than half a percent of Coherent's. By revenue, this is not a David-and-Goliath story. It is a David-and-skyscraper story.

That framing, however, mistakes the competitive question. Sivers is not competing for Coherent's transceiver integration business or Lumentum's optical amplifier franchise. It is positioned — aspirationally, at this stage — at a specific, narrow layer of the supply chain that is structurally reorganising as the industry migrates from pluggable transceivers toward co-packaged optics.

## What Changes at the CPO Layer

In a pluggable transceiver architecture, lasers are effectively commoditised within well-defined categories. Transceivers ship in standard form factors. Customers specify speed and reach; manufacturers produce to catalogue. The large integrated players — Coherent, Lumentum — are optimised for exactly this world, as are the high-volume Japanese generics: Furukawa Electric and Sumitomo Electric, which mass-produce standardised continuous-wave lasers for the bulk transceiver market. Volume, cost efficiency, and yield across millions of units are their competitive axes.

Co-packaged optics disrupts this in a structural way. When lasers move from pluggable modules into the package itself — directly adjacent to the switch silicon — the specification requirements diverge from anything in a standard catalogue. Each customer's interposer geometry, thermal envelope, channel count, and wavelength grid is bespoke. The External Light Source must be tuned to the specific optical platform it feeds. Sivers' own product literature emphasises "customised III-V lasers for specific customer specifications" — language that maps precisely to what POET Technologies, Ayar Labs, and O-Net require from their laser supplier. Whether that custom-specification layer carries durable pricing power against the integrated giants' resources is the open question the chapter cannot resolve.

## The Counterargument Has Substance

Both integrated giants are moving into expanded InP capacity — and faster than the CPO chokepoint thesis would prefer. Coherent disclosed in its FY26 results that it had doubled 6-inch InP wafer output one quarter ahead of its own schedule. Lumentum has acquired a fifth InP fabrication facility in Greensboro, North Carolina, converted from GaAs — a capital commitment unambiguously targeted at expanding custom laser supply. These are not the moves of companies that have ceded the high-specification layer to European design houses.

A further credibility flag on Sivers' own numbers: its PCAOB-restated financials — prepared as part of the US dual-listing process — widened the FY2025 operating loss from SEK 141 million to SEK 178 million and *reduced* FY2024 revenue by SEK 24 million relative to originally reported figures. The restatement drivers included revenue reallocation between periods, revised inventory valuations, and impairment of previously capitalised development expenditures. The accounting gap between Swedish K3 standards and PCAOB requirements is not trivial, and it narrowed the equity base from SEK 1.08 billion to SEK 950 million. Sivers enters the US listing process with a cleaner balance sheet — and a wider disclosed loss.

## The Real Comparable: MACOM, Not Coherent

The more instructive competitive frame is not Coherent or Lumentum but MACOM Technology Solutions — the Lowell, Massachusetts-based photonics semi that occupies a structurally analogous position: a publicly traded laser-chip pure-play with an explicit CPO laser supply positioning, not attempting to compete in transceiver assembly.

| Company | Annual Revenue | Market Cap | Revenue Multiple |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coherent (COHR) | ~$7.2B | ~$19B | ~2.6× |
| Lumentum (LITE) | ~$3.2B | ~$8B | ~2.5× |
| MACOM | ~$700M | ~$10B | ~14× |
| **Sivers Semiconductors** | **~$33M** | **~$2.2B** | **~67×** |

The table captures the core tension. At SEK 72.90 per share across 311.3 million shares outstanding — currently at its five-year high — Sivers is priced at roughly 67 times revenue. To reach MACOM's revenue run-rate, Sivers would need to multiply its top line approximately 20 times. The analyst bull-case model in current specialist investment commentary projects SEK 2.3 billion in 2030 revenue at a 25% operating margin, implying a fair-value estimate of SEK 14.52 per share. The gap to the current market price suggests investors are pricing a scenario considerably more aggressive than even the optimistic case — or pricing a strategic acquisition premium before any acquirer has emerged.

## Geography as an Unpriced Variable

One factor absent from standard comparable-company analysis but material to any complete competitive map is geographic. Sivers is Swedish and British — its photonics subsidiary operates from Glasgow. Coherent is American, with a Swedish operational element. Lumentum and MACOM are both American. Furukawa and Sumitomo are Japanese. From the perspective of a hyperscaler constructing a CPO supply chain for the late 2020s — under conditions of US-China technology bifurcation and potential East Asian supply concentration risk — a European-headquartered independent InP laser source has structural value that does not appear in a discounted cash flow model. The $6.6 million Year 2 grant from the US Microelectronics Commons programme, announced in May 2026, is at least consistent with the thesis that Western government entities view Sivers as a strategic supply option. Whether that optionality justifies a $2.2 billion equity valuation is a separate calculation.

## The Historical Pattern, and What It Requires

The competitive template that Sivers' investment thesis implicitly borrows is well-established in semiconductor history. EML laser specialists who captured the 100G-to-400G transceiver transition built the design-win foundation that became Lumentum's current franchise. Applied Optoelectronics captured disproportionate upside in the 800G and 1.6T transceiver assembler cycle during 2025 by being the right-size, right-specification supplier at the precise moment hyperscalers were racing to lock up bandwidth-density supply. In each case, the winner was not the largest player in the adjacent vertical — it was the one whose specific product specification aligned with the inflection that was actually occurring.

Sivers is positioned at the equivalent inflection for CPO DFB lasers. The preconditions for execution are demanding: a named hyperscaler production order, a successful fab ramp from Glasgow, and a financing structure that avoids forced dilution before revenue arrives. Shares outstanding have already doubled since 2020. The POET partnership — early prototypes expected in H1 2026, production readiness targeted year-end — is the nearest-term test of whether the pattern applies.

The competitive position is asymmetric in both directions. Sivers can lose if Coherent and Lumentum expand custom-laser capability faster than CPO adoption creates lock-in, if Furukawa or Sumitomo upgrade their large-scale production to architectural CW-CPO grades, or if a hyperscaler decides the laser layer is too strategic to outsource. Sivers wins disproportionately to its current revenue base only if one of the POET, Ayar, or O-Net partnerships converts to a named hyperscaler production order before the window narrows. The current market price already assumes a version of that outcome — leaving limited room for the execution risk that the financials, and the restated financials in particular, are signalling is real.

chapters.title: Twelve months of headlines + how the equity story has traveled in specialist commentary
chapters.body:
## The leadership shift that reframed the company

When Sivers replaced Anders Storm with Vickram Vathulya as President and CEO on August 19, 2024, the market took limited notice. The stock was trading below SEK 10. What the appointment signaled — a pivot from engineering-led expansion toward a sharper commercial thesis built around co-packaged optics — would take another year to register in price. Vathulya inherited a company running a SEK 151 million free cash flow deficit in 2022 that had narrowed to SEK 66 million by the time he took the chair; the operational trajectory was improving, but the narrative hadn't yet found its gravity.

## The POET partnership and the re-rating

In 2025, Sivers executed a SEK 95 million rights issue at 8% dilution — the latest in a sequence that has doubled the share count since 2020, a 101.6% cumulative dilution bill for staying alive through the growth stage. The raise was absorbed without visible price damage. Then, on September 29, 2025, came the announcement that repriced the equity story: a [strategic collaboration with POET Technologies](https://www.poet-technologies.com/news/poet-technologies-and-sivers-semiconductors-collaborate-on-external-light-sources-for-co-packaged-optics-and-next-generation-ai-market) to co-develop External Light Source modules for co-packaged optics and AI infrastructure — Sivers' high-power InP DFB lasers mated to POET's Optical Interposer platform.

> "We see a highly complementary fit between our high-performance DFB lasers and POET's innovative optical interposer platform." — Vickram Vathulya, September 2025

Needham analyst Tim Savageaux has pegged the ELS addressable market at over $1 billion annually, within a broader AI optical connectivity opportunity exceeding $50 billion. Early prototypes were targeted for H1 2026; production readiness for end-2026. Those milestones have not yet been validated by shipped revenue. The market did not wait: the stock accelerated sharply through Q4 2025 as the CPO pure-play thesis consolidated around Sivers as the InP laser foundry that neither POET, Ayar Labs, nor O-Net can replicate internally.

## The restatement: tighter accounting, wider losses

On February 26, 2026, preliminary full-year results arrived: SEK 306.6 million in revenue, up 25% year-on-year (33% in constant currency), against an operating loss of SEK 177.8 million. Cash at year-end stood at a thin SEK 43.5 million. Simultaneously, the company raised $17 million in term loans and convertible debt — the lender not publicly identified — to extend its runway.

The fuller reckoning came on [May 13, 2026](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/press/sivers-semiconductors-publishes-the-2025-annual-report-adjusting-prior-reported-financials-as-preparation-for-a-potential-dual-listing-in-the-united-states/), when Sivers published a PCAOB-aligned Annual Report — delayed from its original target — carrying restated figures materially worse than first reported. The EBIT loss widened from SEK -141.3 million to SEK -177.8 million; the net loss from SEK -186.5 million to SEK -222.6 million; EPS deteriorated from SEK -0.69 to SEK -0.81. Restatement drivers included revenue reallocation between periods (some deferred into 2026 and beyond), revised inventory valuations, and impairment of previously capitalised development costs. FY2024 was also revised: revenue fell from SEK 243.7 million to SEK 219.2 million, and the net loss widened from SEK -116.3 million to SEK -183.9 million. Under PCAOB standards, two years of historical performance look materially softer than Swedish K3 accounting had implied.

## May 2026: grants, governance, and an open investigation

Six days after the annual report, Sivers announced a $6.6 million [NEMC Year 2 grant](https://www.sivers-semiconductors.com/investors/) from the US Department of Defense's Microelectronics Commons program. The sum is modest relative to a SEK 66 million free cash flow deficit; its strategic function is to establish Sivers Photonics as a dual-use domestic compound semiconductor asset — positioning that matters acutely for a company preparing a potential US listing.

Board nominations for the June 15 AGM followed on May 20: Joakim Nideborn and Helena Svancar proposed as new directors. The same meeting will vote on a 15% dilution authority and will see Erik Fällström — who controls approximately 11.8% of votes via DDM Debt and his family office — step down. Fällström has publicly favoured moving Sivers toward a "broader investment company"; his departure removes a tension point incompatible with the pure-play operational identity a US listing requires. Sweden's Ekobrottsmyndigheten insider trading investigation remains open as of the snapshot date; no charges have been filed.

Forward catalysts within 90-180 days: Q1 2026 results (originally scheduled May 29, delayed at snapshot), the June 15 AGM, a potential Nasdaq dual-listing announcement, and the POET prototype demonstration. Into H2 2026-2027: POET production readiness at year-end and an unnamed automotive LiDAR customer's ramp in Q4 2026 — a contract valued at SEK 530–1,420 million over its lifetime (16-44% of FY2025 revenue). None of these has been de-risked.

## How the equity story has traveled in specialist commentary

The stock's 40x move since its SEK 1.80 five-year low — it touched SEK 72.90 at the snapshot date, a five-year high — has generated sustained retail attention on X/Twitter. The account @aleabitoreddit has published approximately 385 posts on Sivers across 2025-2026, making it among the most prolific trackers of the name in the specialist commentary ecosystem.

One widely-followed retail-side commentator has pattern-matched Sivers explicitly to Lumentum's 2024 trajectory — positioning this as the moment LITE occupied before hyperscaler design-in announcements triggered a re-rating. The comparison is structurally consistent: COHR, LITE, and Sivers occupy adjacent tiers in the same optical interconnect supply chain, all upstream of the hyperscaler integration layer. But the timing of any LITE-style re-rating depends on announcements — from NVIDIA, Microsoft, Meta, or Amazon naming Sivers via an integrator — that have not yet occurred. The POET collaboration is the nearest thing to a named-hyperscaler adjacency in the public record. Until a production design win is confirmed at the integrator or hyperscaler level, the CPO chokepoint thesis remains a bet on supply-chain position, not a validated order book.

chapters.title: InP DFB lasers — patents, products, and the case for chokepoint pricing
chapters.body:
The IP density question is the right place to start, because the entire investment case for Sivers rests on it. If Sivers holds a genuine chokepoint in the laser supply chain for co-packaged optics, it commands pricing power and customer stickiness. If it doesn't — if sufficiently motivated competitors can replicate its InP DFB process within a product cycle — then it's simply a modestly sized fabricator with a temporarily favorable order book.

The patent portfolio offers one data point, albeit an incomplete one. Public patent databases show Sivers Photonics holding three issued patents and 16 applications pending across US, UK, Canada, and WIPO jurisdictions. The USPTO has issued patents including *Distributed feedback laser having enhanced etch stop features* and *Method of making an InP-based DFB laser* — both titles signalling process-level IP rather than end-product claims. The company describes itself as "one of the world's most advanced designer[s] (and small scale manufacturer) of customised III-V lasers," a characterization drawn from its own corporate literature.

Against this, consider the competitive baseline: Coherent and Lumentum each hold hundreds of issued laser patents. Measured by count alone, Sivers' 19 total filings look thin. But that comparison misfires. Coherent and Lumentum built their portfolios around volume production of standard telecom lasers — DWDM line cards, transceiver modules. That IP doesn't meaningfully cover what Sivers is doing: continuous-wave InP DFB designs optimized for the high-power, narrow-linewidth requirements of silicon photonics integration, specifically in the C-band (1530–1565nm) window required for co-packaged optics in AI datacenter switches.

## The Three-Layer Technical Stack

To understand why the IP picture matters differently here, you need to understand what Sivers actually builds. The chokepoint isn't a single component — it's the integrated capability to execute across three distinct technical disciplines simultaneously.
